content: Cigarette smoking significantly increases the risk of severe side effects associated with oral contraceptives, such as heart attacks, blood clots, and strokes. This risk is particularly elevated in women over the age of 35 who smoke heavily (15 or more cigarettes per day). If you are taking oral contraceptives, you should not smoke. Oral contraceptives, commonly known as birth control pills, are prescribed to prevent pregnancy. These medications contain two female sex hormones, estrogen and progestin, which work together to inhibit ovulation (the release of eggs from the ovaries). Additionally, they alter the uterine lining to prevent implantation and modify cervical mucus to block sperm from entering the uterus. While highly effective at preventing pregnancy, oral contraceptives do not protect against sexually transmitted infections, including HIV. Certain brands of oral contraceptives are also used to treat acne by reducing levels of specific natural substances that contribute to acne formation. Oral contraceptives are available in packets containing 21, 28, or 91 tablets. They are taken orally once daily, following a regular schedule. To minimize nausea, it is recommended to take the pill with food or milk and at the same time each day. Follow the instructions on your prescription label carefully, and consult your doctor or pharmacist if you have any questions. Do not alter the dosage or frequency of the medication without your doctor’s approval. Different brands of oral contraceptives may contain varying medications, doses, and instructions for use, as well as differing risks and benefits. Ensure you understand the specific brand you are using and its proper usage. If you have a 21-tablet packet, take one tablet daily for 21 days, followed by a 7-day break before starting a new packet. For a 28-tablet packet, take one tablet daily for 28 days. The last set of tablets in most 28-day packets are reminder pills, which may not contain active ingredients but help you maintain your schedule. Some 28-day packets contain only active tablets, all of the same color. Regardless of the type, take one tablet daily in the specified order and start a new packet immediately after finishing the previous one. If you are using a 91-day packet, take one tablet daily for 91 days, following the order specified in the packet. The last set of tablets may contain inactive ingredients or a low dose of estrogen. Begin a new packet the day after completing the 91st tablet. Your doctor will advise you on when to start taking oral contraceptives, typically on the first or fifth day of your menstrual period or the first Sunday after bleeding begins. They may also recommend using an additional birth control method during the first 7 days of taking the pill. Withdrawal bleeding, similar to a menstrual period, may occur while taking inactive or low-dose estrogen tablets or during the week you do not take the pill. If your packet contains only active tablets, you may not experience scheduled bleeding but could have unexpected spotting, especially at the start of treatment. Begin your new packet on schedule, even if you are still bleeding. If you vomit or have diarrhea while taking oral contraceptives, you may need a backup birth control method. Discuss this with your doctor beforehand to prepare for such situations. If you have recently given birth, wait at least 4 weeks before starting oral contraceptives. If you have had an abortion or miscarriage, consult your doctor about when to begin taking the pill. Oral contraceptives are effective only when taken consistently. Continue taking them daily, even if you experience spotting, nausea, or other minor side effects. Do not stop taking the medication without consulting your doctor. Oral contraceptives may also be prescribed for conditions such as heavy or irregular menstruation and endometriosis, a condition where uterine-like tissue grows outside the uterus, causing pain and other symptoms. Discuss the risks and benefits of using this medication for your condition with your doctor. Before starting oral contraceptives, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to estrogen, progestin, or any other medications. Provide a complete list of all prescription and nonprescription medications, vitamins, and supplements you are taking, as certain drugs may interact with oral contraceptives. These include, but are not limited to, anticoagulants, antifungals, seizure medications, HIV protease inhibitors, and herbal products like St. John’s wort. Your doctor may need to adjust your medication doses or monitor you for side effects. Inform your doctor if you have a history of blood clots, heart disease, stroke, high blood pressure, diabetes, liver disease, breast cancer, or other significant medical conditions. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, do not take oral contraceptives. If you miss a period while taking the pill, consult your doctor, as you may be pregnant. Follow specific instructions for missed doses provided with your medication, and use a backup birth control method if necessary. Oral contraceptives may cause minor side effects such as nausea, vomiting, bloating, weight changes, or spotting between periods. Report severe side effects, including intense headaches, chest pain, vision changes, or signs of blood clots, to your doctor immediately. Oral contraceptives may increase the risk of liver tumors, breast or liver cancer, heart attack, stroke, or serious blood clots. Discuss these risks with your doctor. Store oral contraceptives in their original packaging at room temperature, away from heat and moisture. Dispose of expired or unused medication properly. In case of overdose, contact a poison control center or emergency services immediately. Keep all medical appointments and undergo regular physical exams, including blood pressure checks and breast and pelvic exams. If you wish to stop taking oral contraceptives to become pregnant, consult your doctor about alternative birth control methods and the potential delay in returning to regular menstruation. Oral contraceptives may reduce folate levels, so discuss supplementation with your doctor if planning a pregnancy. Do not share your medication with others, and consult your pharmacist for any questions about refills.
